subject: physics
title: Momentum, Impulse and Collisions
welcome_lead: Conserve momentum through explosions and collisions, and use impulse to handle changing forces.
meta_desc: A-Level Mechanics adventure on momentum, impulse and collision analysis.
final_note: Momentum is always conserved in closed systems — kinetic energy only sometimes.

concepts.def: Product of mass and velocity: p = mv.
Change in momentum: J = F·t = Δp.
Collision where kinetic energy is conserved.

Total momentum before equals total after.

walkthroughs.body_html: Impulse J = F·Δt = Δp = m(v - u). A large force for short time and a small force for long time can give the same impulse — that's why crumple zones work.
m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2. Treat directions with signs. For perfectly inelastic: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = (m1+m2) v.
Calculate ½mv² before and after. If KE is conserved the collision is elastic. If KE drops, energy went to deformation, heat or sound.

mcqs.q: In a collision between two objects, what quantity is always conserved (in a closed system)?
options: Total momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.
Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions because energy is conserved.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.

mcqs.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot water heat up faster than a wooden one?
options: Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Metals have higher thermal conductivity, so heat is transferred more rapidly through them.
Metal heats up faster because it has a lower specific heat capacity, requiring less energy per degree.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.

mcqs.q: When energy is 'lost' as heat due to friction, what has really happened?
options: Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
Energy has been used up and no longer exists.
Energy has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings — it's not destroyed, just dissipated.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
